questions.stem: Non-allelic homologous recombination between segmental duplications in opposite orientation on the same chromosome produces:
questions.explanation: Inverted repeats recombine to flip the intervening segment. A, B: Direct repeats yield deletions or duplications. D: SDs on different chromosomes yield translocations. E: NAHR causes structural, not point, changes.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old has slowly progressive distal leg weakness; nerve conduction studies show a demyelinating neuropathy, and he is diagnosed with Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A. Which genetic change is most likely?
questions.explanation: Most CMT1A is a 1.5-Mb chr17 duplication including PMP22, produced by NAHR between flanking segmental duplications. A: A single PMP22 copy causes HNPP. C: The classic mechanism changes PMP22 dosage; a translocation doesn't. D: Inversions don't change dosage. E: Chromothripsis is a complex multi-rearrangement event, not the usual cause.

questions.stem: Which abnormality would a chromosomal microarray (array-CGH) detect?
questions.explanation: Microarrays detect copy-number changes larger than ~1 kb. A: A balanced translocation has no gain or loss. B: An inversion is balanced too. C: Far below ~1-kb resolution; sequencing is needed. E: Also below the resolution.

questions.stem: Which abnormality is most likely to be missed by a standard karyotype?
questions.explanation: Standard karyotyping resolves only changes >5 Mb; a 1-Mb deletion needs a microarray (>1 kb resolution). A: A whole extra chromosome is visible. B: Large translocations are visible. C: Large inversions are visible. D: Ring chromosomes are visible.

questions.stem: Exome sequencing is done for a child with a rare disease. Which variant is most likely removed at the first filtering step?

options.D: A rare homozygous missense variant in a known disease gene

questions.explanation: The first filter removes common variants (minor allele frequency >1%), which are unlikely to cause a rare disease. A: Rare and predicted damaging, so kept. C: Novel and truncating, so kept. D: Rare and in a disease gene, so kept. E: Rare and predicted damaging, so kept.

questions.stem: Which DNA repair pathway joins double-strand break ends with little or no homology, often leaving small insertions or deletions?
questions.explanation: NHEJ fuses double-strand break ends with little or no homology, especially in G0/G1, leaving insertions or deletions at the junction. B: NAHR needs highly identical segmental duplications. C: FoSTeS is a replication error, not break repair. D: Serial replication slippage is also replication-based. E: Crossing-over is normal meiotic exchange between non-sister chromatids.

questions.stem: Two 15-kb regions on the same chromosome share 97% sequence identity. How are they best classified?
questions.explanation: SDs/LCRs are regions ≥1 kb present in more than one copy with ≥90% identity; they mediate NAHR. B: STRs have 2–5-bp repeat units. C: SINEs are <500 bp. D: VNTR units are 10–100 bp. E: LINEs are ~6 kb interspersed retrotransposons.
